meta.topic: 线性代数：矩阵微分、梯度恒等式、最优化、谱导数、矩阵函数与反向传播

zh:
设 $f:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}$ 在 $x$ 处可微。按本批统一的分母（梯度）布局，定义 $
abla f(x)\in\mathbb{R}^n$ 为列向量，其第 $j$ 个分量为 $\partial f/\partial x_j$。由可微性的一阶展开，对任意 $dx\in\mathbb{R}^n$，$$f(x+dx)=f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^n rac{\partial f}{\partial x_j}\,dx_j+o(\|dx\|).$$ 右端线性项等于 $(
abla f)^{	op}dx$，故 $df=(
abla f)^{	op}dx$。结论：标量对向量的导数与 $x$ 同型，是列向量；条件是可微性，$dx$ 任意。

设 $y:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ 在 $x$ 处可微。定义雅可比矩阵 $J=\partial y/\partial x\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$，其第 $(i,j)$ 元为 $\partial y_i/\partial x_j$。对每个分量作一阶展开并忽略 $o(\|dx\|)$，得 $dy_i=\sum_j J_{ij}dx_j$，合并为 $dy=J\,dx$；因此 $J$ 的第 $i$ 行是 $(\nabla y_i)^{\top}$。当 $m=1$ 时 $J$ 是 $1\times n$ 行向量，恰为标量梯度列向量的转置——这正是混合布局中两种情形的衔接处。结论：向量对向量取标准 $m\times n$ 雅可比（行对应输出分量）。

设 $f:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to\mathbb{R}$ 在 $X$ 处可微，定义 $G\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ 的 $(i,j)$ 元为 $\partial f/\partial X_{ij}$。全微分是 $$df=\sum_{i,j}G_{ij}\,dX_{ij}.$$ 由于 $(G^{\top}dX)_{jj}=\sum_i G_{ij}dX_{ij}$，对 $j$ 求和得 $\operatorname{tr}(G^{\top}dX)=\sum_{i,j}G_{ij}dX_{ij}$，所以 $df=\operatorname{tr}(G^{\top}dX)$。反过来，若对某个 $H$ 有 $df=\operatorname{tr}(H^{\top}dX)$ 对一切 $dX$ 成立，取 $dX=E_{ij}$ 得 $H_{ij}=$ 该方向导数 $=G_{ij}$，故 $H=G$ 唯一。结论：标量对矩阵的导数与 $X$ 同型，且迹形式与逐元素定义等价。

沿任意方向 $B$ 取路径 $X(t)=X+tB$，由链式法则 $\frac{d}{dt}\big|_{0}f(X+tB)=\operatorname{tr}(G^{\top}B)$，等价地 $$f(X+tB)=f(X)+t\,\operatorname{tr}(G^{\top}B)+o(t).$$ 向量情形同理：$f(x+td)=f(x)+t(\nabla f)^{\top}d+o(t)$。这说明导数是一个关于方向线性的泛函，而 $G$ 正是它在迹内积下的表示；也给出有限差分检验：用 $(f(X+tE_{ij})-f(X))/t$ 逼近 $G_{ij}$。条件是 $f$ 可微、$t\to0$。

例：$f(X)=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\top}X)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}X_{ij}$。直接微分得 $df=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\top}dX)$，与 $df=\operatorname{tr}(G^{\top}dX)$ 对照即 $G=A$；取 $dX=E_{ij}$ 也得到方向导数 $A_{ij}$。若写成 $f(X)=\operatorname{tr}(AX)$，则 $df=\operatorname{tr}(A\,dX)$，对照识别式得梯度 $A^{\top}$，顺序与转置不能混。结论：识别 $G$ 时只需把 $df$ 凑成迹形式，系数矩阵要连同转置一起读。

布局换算：若某文献用分子布局，把标量对向量的导数写成行向量 $r^{\top}$，则本批的列梯度是 $r$；标量对矩阵的分子布局结果 $H_{\text{num}}$ 与本批的 $G_{\text{den}}$ 互为转置，$H_{\text{num}}=G_{\text{den}}^{\top}$。向量对向量的雅可比还必须核对取向：只有当对方也满足 $dy=J\,dx$ 且 $J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ 时才与本批一致，否则先转置。结论：全篇统一「标量按分母布局、向量对向量按标准雅可比」；引用任何公式前先确认约定，且一次推导内不得混用。
en:
Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $x$. Under the batch-wide denominator (gradient) layout, define $
abla f(x)\in\mathbb{R}^n$ as the column vector whose $j$-th entry is $\partial f/\partial x_j$. Differentiability gives, for every $dx\in\mathbb{R}^n$, $$f(x+dx)=f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^n rac{\partial f}{\partial x_j}\,dx_j+o(\|dx\|).$$ The linear term equals $(
abla f)^{	op}dx$, hence $df=(
abla f)^{	op}dx$. Conclusion: the derivative of a scalar with respect to a vector has the same shape as $x$ and is a column vector; the hypothesis is differentiability and $dx$ is arbitrary.

Let $y:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ be differentiable at $x$, and define the Jacobian $J=\partial y/\partial x\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ by $J_{ij}=\partial y_i/\partial x_j$. Expanding each component to first order and dropping $o(\|dx\|)$ gives $dy_i=\sum_j J_{ij}dx_j$, hence $dy=J\,dx$; the $i$-th row of $J$ is $(\nabla y_i)^{\top}$. For $m=1$, $J$ is a $1\times n$ row, exactly the transpose of the scalar gradient column — this is where the two cases of the mixed layout meet. Conclusion: vector-by-vector derivatives use the standard $m\times n$ Jacobian (rows indexed by outputs).

Let $f:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to\mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $X$, and define $G\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ by $G_{ij}=\partial f/\partial X_{ij}$. The total differential is $$df=\sum_{i,j}G_{ij}\,dX_{ij}.$$ Since $(G^{\top}dX)_{jj}=\sum_i G_{ij}dX_{ij}$, summing over $j$ gives $\operatorname{tr}(G^{\top}dX)=\sum_{i,j}G_{ij}dX_{ij}$, hence $df=\operatorname{tr}(G^{\top}dX)$. Conversely, if $df=\operatorname{tr}(H^{\top}dX)$ for all $dX$, testing $dX=E_{ij}$ gives $H_{ij}=$ the directional derivative $=G_{ij}$, so $H=G$ is unique. Conclusion: a scalar-by-matrix derivative has the same shape as $X$, and the trace form is equivalent to the entrywise definition.

Along any direction $B$, take $X(t)=X+tB$. The chain rule gives $\frac{d}{dt}\big|_{0}f(X+tB)=\operatorname{tr}(G^{\top}B)$, equivalently $$f(X+tB)=f(X)+t\,\operatorname{tr}(G^{\top}B)+o(t).$$ The vector case is analogous: $f(x+td)=f(x)+t(\nabla f)^{\top}d+o(t)$. Thus the derivative is a linear functional of the direction, and $G$ represents it in the trace inner product; this also yields the finite-difference test $(f(X+tE_{ij})-f(X))/t\to G_{ij}$. The hypotheses are differentiability and $t\to0$.

Example: $f(X)=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\top}X)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}X_{ij}$. Direct differentiation gives $df=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\top}dX)$, and comparison with $df=\operatorname{tr}(G^{\top}dX)$ yields $G=A$; testing $dX=E_{ij}$ also gives the directional derivative $A_{ij}$. If instead $f(X)=\operatorname{tr}(AX)$, then $df=\operatorname{tr}(A\,dX)$, and the identification rule gives the gradient $A^{\top}$; order and transpose cannot be mixed up. Conclusion: to identify $G$, put $df$ into trace form and read the coefficient together with its transpose.

Layout conversion: if a source uses the numerator layout and writes the scalar-by-vector derivative as a row $r^{\top}$, then the column gradient in this batch is $r$; for scalar-by-matrix derivatives, the numerator-layout result $H_{\text{num}}$ and the denominator-layout result $G_{\text{den}}$ satisfy $H_{\text{num}}=G_{\text{den}}^{\top}$. Vector-by-vector Jacobians also need an orientation check: they agree with this batch only when $dy=J\,dx$ with $J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$; otherwise transpose first. Conclusion: use one convention throughout — denominator layout for scalars and the standard Jacobian for vector-by-vector — and never mix conventions within a derivation.

zh: 把矩阵看成单参数族 $X(t)$，定义 $dF=\frac{d}{dt}\big|_{0}F(X(t))$（差一个 $dt$ 的标量因子）；也可直接把它理解为沿任意方向 $B$ 的方向导数。$d$ 是线性算子：$$d(X+Y)=dX+dY,\qquad d(kX)=k\,dX,\qquad d(X^{\top})=(dX)^{\top}.$$ 又因迹是线性的，$d\operatorname{tr}X=\operatorname{tr}(dX)$。条件是相关元素可微、形状相容。结论：加法、数乘、转置与迹都可以逐项穿过 $d$。

乘积法则由路径乘积求导得到：$$d(XY)=\frac{d}{dt}\big|_{0}\big(X(t)Y(t)\big)=(dX)Y+X\,dY.$$ 两个因子的左右位置必须保持；三因子情形为 $d(XYZ)=(dX)YZ+X(dY)Z+XY(dZ)$。Hadamard 乘积逐元素就是标量乘积，故 $d(X\odot Y)=(dX)\odot Y+X\odot dY$。条件是乘法或 Hadamard 乘积形状相容、元素可微。结论：矩阵乘法不交换，微分时不能把 $(dX)Y$ 写成 $Y(dX)$。

设 $X$ 在讨论点可逆。对恒等式 $XX^{-1}=I$ 两边取 $d$，用乘积法则得 $$(dX)X^{-1}+X\,d(X^{-1})=0,$$ 左乘 $X^{-1}$ 即得 $$d(X^{-1})=-X^{-1}(dX)X^{-1}.$$ 这里 $dX$ 被夹在三个因子中间，顺序不能反；$-X^{-2}dX$ 或 $-(dX)X^{-2}$ 只有在 $dX$ 与 $X$ 可交换时才可能碰巧成立，一般情形是错的。可逆性在一点成立时由连续性在邻域内保持，故路径导数同样成立。结论：逆的微分公式为 $d(X^{-1})=-X^{-1}dX\,X^{-1}$。

迹的微分就是 $d\operatorname{tr}X=\operatorname{tr}(dX)$；对 $f(X)=\operatorname{tr}(AX)$ 有 $df=\operatorname{tr}(A\,dX)$。若 $P\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$、$Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$，则 $$\operatorname{tr}(PQ)=\sum_{i,j}P_{ij}Q_{ji}=\operatorname{tr}(QP),$$ 多因子时只能循环移动，$\operatorname{tr}(PQR)=\operatorname{tr}(RPQ)$（形状相容时）。条件：每个迹的自变量为方阵。结论：迹的循环性是把 $dX$ 挪到末尾、从而读出梯度的关键工具，但不能任意交换因子顺序。

行列式的一般微分：固定一行 $i$ 作余子式展开 $\det X=\sum_j X_{ij}C_{ij}$，其中余子式 $C_{ij}$ 不含 $X_{ij}$，故 $\partial\det X/\partial X_{ij}=C_{ij}=(\operatorname{adj}X)_{ji}$。于是 $$\begin{aligned}d\det X&=\sum_{i,j}(\operatorname{adj}X)_{ji}dX_{ij}\\&=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(X)\,dX).\end{aligned}$$ 对任意方阵成立。当 $X$ 可逆时 $\operatorname{adj}(X)=\det(X)X^{-1}$，代入得 $$d\det X=\det(X)\,\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}dX).$$ 条件：第一式只要求 $X$ 为方阵，第二式额外要求 $X$ 可逆。结论：含 $X^{-1}$ 的简洁形式不能用于奇异矩阵。

复合函数用「先内后外」：设 $Y=Y(X)$、$f=f(Y)$ 均可微。先算内层 $dY$，再代入外层 $$df=\operatorname{tr}\left(\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial Y}\right)^{\top}dY\right),$$ 用循环性把 $dY$ 中的 $dX$ 归并到迹的末尾，写成 $df=\operatorname{tr}(G^{\top}dX)$，则 $G=\partial f/\partial X$。例如 $f=\operatorname{tr}(AX^{-1})$：令 $Y=X^{-1}$，则 $\partial f/\partial Y=A^{\top}$、$dY=-Y\,dX\,Y$，于是 $df=-\operatorname{tr}(A Y\,dX\,Y)=-\operatorname{tr}(Y A Y\,dX)$，读出 $G=-Y^{\top}A^{\top}Y^{\top}=-X^{-\top}A^{\top}X^{-\top}$（$X$ 可逆）。结论：链式流程不需要额外的矩阵链式法则公式，只需内层微分、回代与迹的循环。
en: View a matrix as a one-parameter family $X(t)$ and define $dF=\frac{d}{dt}\big|_{0}F(X(t))$ (up to the scalar factor $dt$); equivalently, read it as the directional derivative along an arbitrary direction $B$. The operator $d$ is linear: $$d(X+Y)=dX+dY,\qquad d(kX)=k\,dX,\qquad d(X^{\top})=(dX)^{\top}.$$ Since the trace is linear, $d\operatorname{tr}X=\operatorname{tr}(dX)$. The hypotheses are differentiability of the entries and compatible shapes. Conclusion: addition, scalar multiplication, transposition and the trace all pass through $d$ termwise.

The product rule comes from differentiating a path of products: $$d(XY)=\frac{d}{dt}\big|_{0}\big(X(t)Y(t)\big)=(dX)Y+X\,dY.$$ The left-right positions of the factors must be preserved; for three factors, $d(XYZ)=(dX)YZ+X(dY)Z+XY(dZ)$. The Hadamard product is entrywise, so $d(X\odot Y)=(dX)\odot Y+X\odot dY$. The hypotheses are compatible shapes for the product or Hadamard product and differentiability. Conclusion: matrix multiplication does not commute, so $(dX)Y$ must not be rewritten as $Y(dX)$.

Assume $X$ is invertible at the point under discussion. Applying $d$ to $XX^{-1}=I$ and using the product rule gives $$(dX)X^{-1}+X\,d(X^{-1})=0,$$ and left multiplication by $X^{-1}$ yields $$d(X^{-1})=-X^{-1}(dX)X^{-1}.$$ Here $dX$ is sandwiched between three factors and the order is essential; $-X^{-2}dX$ or $-(dX)X^{-2}$ can hold only accidentally when $dX$ commutes with $X$, and is wrong in general. Invertibility at one point persists in a neighborhood by continuity, so the same formula holds along paths. Conclusion: $d(X^{-1})=-X^{-1}dX\,X^{-1}$.

The differential of the trace is $d\operatorname{tr}X=\operatorname{tr}(dX)$; for $f(X)=\operatorname{tr}(AX)$, $df=\operatorname{tr}(A\,dX)$. If $P\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$, then $$\operatorname{tr}(PQ)=\sum_{i,j}P_{ij}Q_{ji}=\operatorname{tr}(QP),$$ and with several factors only cyclic shifts are allowed: $\operatorname{tr}(PQR)=\operatorname{tr}(RPQ)$ when the shapes are compatible. The hypothesis is that every trace argument is square. Conclusion: cyclicity is the key tool for moving $dX$ to the end and reading off the gradient, but factors cannot be permuted arbitrarily.

General determinant differential: expand along a fixed row $i$, $\det X=\sum_j X_{ij}C_{ij}$, where the cofactor $C_{ij}$ does not contain $X_{ij}$; hence $\partial\det X/\partial X_{ij}=C_{ij}=(\operatorname{adj}X)_{ji}$. Therefore $$\begin{aligned}d\det X&=\sum_{i,j}(\operatorname{adj}X)_{ji}dX_{ij}\\&=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(X)\,dX).\end{aligned}$$ valid for every square matrix. If $X$ is invertible, $\operatorname{adj}(X)=\det(X)X^{-1}$, and substitution gives $$d\det X=\det(X)\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}dX).$$ The first identity needs only a square $X$; the second additionally needs invertibility. Conclusion: the compact form containing $X^{-1}$ cannot be used for singular matrices.

For composites, work “inner first”: let $Y=Y(X)$ and $f=f(Y)$ be differentiable. Compute the inner differential $dY$, substitute it into the outer differential $$df=\operatorname{tr}\left(\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial Y}\right)^{\top}dY\right),$$ then use cyclicity to collect $dX$ at the end of the trace and write $df=\operatorname{tr}(G^{\top}dX)$; then $G=\partial f/\partial X$. For example, for $f=\operatorname{tr}(AX^{-1})$, set $Y=X^{-1}$; then $\partial f/\partial Y=A^{\top}$ and $dY=-Y\,dX\,Y$, so $df=-\operatorname{tr}(A Y\,dX\,Y)=-\operatorname{tr}(Y A Y\,dX)$, giving $G=-Y^{\top}A^{\top}Y^{\top}=-X^{-\top}A^{\top}X^{-\top}$ for invertible $X$. Conclusion: the chain workflow needs no separate matrix chain-rule formula — only the inner differential, substitution and trace cyclicity.

zh: 目标是把 $df$ 写成 $\operatorname{tr}(G^{\top}dX)$，然后读出 $G=\partial f/\partial X$；向量情形则写成 $(\nabla f)^{\top}dx$。操作固定为三步：① 用乘积、逆、行列式、迹的法则展开 $df$；② 用 $\operatorname{tr}(PQR)=\operatorname{tr}(RPQ)$ 把 $dX$ 移到迹的末尾；③ 把 $dX$ 前的系数整体看成 $G^{\top}$，转置得到 $G$。条件是 $f$ 在 $X$ 处可微、所有迹的形状相容；分母布局保证 $G$ 与 $X$ 同型。结论：所有条目都可以现场重推，不必死记。

线性迹型：$f=\operatorname{tr}(AX)$，则 $$df=\operatorname{tr}(A\,dX)=\operatorname{tr}\big((A^{\top})^{\top}dX\big),$$ 故 $\partial\operatorname{tr}(AX)/\partial X=A^{\top}$。这不是 $A$：转置来自识别式中的 $G^{\top}$。同理 $\operatorname{tr}(AX^{\top})$ 的微分为 $\operatorname{tr}(A(dX)^{\top})=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\top}dX)$，故其梯度为 $A$；$\operatorname{tr}X$ 的梯度为 $I$。对 $\operatorname{tr}(AX)$ 要求 $A$ 为 $m\times n$、$X$ 为 $n\times m$；对 $\operatorname{tr}(AX^{\top})$ 要求 $A,X$ 同为 $m\times n$。两者都不要求方阵，只要迹有定义。结论：迹线性型的系数矩阵在读出梯度时要转置，$A^{\top}$ 与 $A$ 的位置不能凭记忆混用。

二次型与双线性型。对 $f(x)=x^{\top}Ax$，$$\begin{aligned}df&=(dx)^{\top}Ax+x^{\top}A\,dx\\&=x^{\top}A^{\top}dx+x^{\top}A\,dx\\&=x^{\top}(A+A^{\top})dx.\end{aligned}$$ 故 $\nabla f=(A+A^{\top})x$；只有 $A=A^{\top}$ 时才简化为 $2Ax$。对 $f(X)=a^{\top}Xb$，$$\begin{aligned}df&=a^{\top}(dX)b=\operatorname{tr}(ba^{\top}dX)\\&=\operatorname{tr}\big((ab^{\top})^{\top}dX\big).\end{aligned}$$ 故 $\partial(a^{\top}Xb)/\partial X=ab^{\top}$。条件是 $A$ 为 $n\times n$ 实矩阵、$a,b$ 与 $X$ 形状相容；二次型公式不要求 $A$ 对称，但必须对称化。结论：外积 $ab^{\top}$ 与对称化后的 $(A+A^{\top})x$ 是两张基本表。

迹二次型：设 $A$ 为 $n\times n$、$X$ 为 $n\times p$，$f=\operatorname{tr}(X^{\top}AX)$。则 $$\begin{aligned}df&=\operatorname{tr}\big((dX)^{\top}AX\big)+\operatorname{tr}\big(X^{\top}A\,dX\big)\\&=\operatorname{tr}\big(X^{\top}A^{\top}dX\big)+\operatorname{tr}\big(X^{\top}A\,dX\big)\\&=\operatorname{tr}\big(((A+A^{\top})X)^{\top}dX\big),\end{aligned}$$ 故梯度为 $(A+A^{\top})X$；$A$ 对称时为 $2AX$。第一步用了 $\operatorname{tr}((dX)^{\top}AX)=\operatorname{tr}(X^{\top}A^{\top}dX)$（标量转置不变），最后一步用了 $(A+A^{\top})X$ 的转置。条件：形状相容、$f$ 可微。结论：无论 $X$ 是向量还是矩阵，二次型的梯度都要先对称化 $A$。

行列式与逆型（$X$ 可逆）。由 Jacobi 公式 $d\det X=\det X\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}dX)$，而 $\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}dX)=\operatorname{tr}((X^{-\top})^{\top}dX)$，故 $$\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial\det X}{\partial X}&=\det(X)\,X^{-\top},\\ \frac{\partial\ln\det X}{\partial X}&=X^{-\top}.\end{aligned}$$ 对 $f=\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}A)$，用 $d(X^{-1})=-X^{-1}dX\,X^{-1}$：$$df=-\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}dX\,X^{-1}A)=-\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}AX^{-1}dX),$$ 故 $\partial f/\partial X=-X^{-\top}A^{\top}X^{-\top}$。条件：$X$ 可逆（$\ln\det$ 还要求 $\det X>0$ 以取实对数，例如 $X$ 正定）。结论：逆型公式的两个转置都不能漏。

两个易错点。其一，上面的 $\partial\det X/\partial X$ 与 $\partial\ln\det X/\partial X$ 是**无约束**（整个矩阵空间）版本；若把 $X$ 限制在对称矩阵上，切空间只剩对称方向，内在梯度应取对称部分 $\operatorname{sym}(G)=(G+G^{\top})/2$，因为 $\operatorname{tr}(G^{\top}dX)$ 只看见 $dX$ 的对称部分。对对称可逆 $X$，$\det X\,X^{-\top}=\det X\,X^{-1}$ 已经对称，故该条不变；但 $\operatorname{tr}(AX)$ 在对称子空间上的内在梯度是 $(A+A^{\top})/2$，不是 $A^{\top}$。其二，任何结果都可用有限差分核对：任取 $B$，比较 $(f(X+tB)-f(X))/t$ 与 $\operatorname{tr}(G^{\top}B)$。条件：约束流形上的内积与切空间必须固定。结论：先确认是否无约束，再套公式。
en: The goal is to write $df$ as $\operatorname{tr}(G^{\top}dX)$ and then read off $G=\partial f/\partial X$; in the vector case, write $df=(\nabla f)^{\top}dx$. The procedure has three steps: (i) expand $df$ using the product, inverse, determinant and trace rules; (ii) use $\operatorname{tr}(PQR)=\operatorname{tr}(RPQ)$ to move $dX$ to the end of the trace; (iii) regard the coefficient of $dX$ as $G^{\top}$ and transpose it to obtain $G$. The hypotheses are differentiability of $f$ at $X$ and compatible trace shapes; the denominator layout guarantees that $G$ has the shape of $X$. Conclusion: every entry can be re-derived on the spot, with no need for memorization.

Linear trace forms: for $f=\operatorname{tr}(AX)$, $$df=\operatorname{tr}(A\,dX)=\operatorname{tr}\big((A^{\top})^{\top}dX\big),$$ so $\partial\operatorname{tr}(AX)/\partial X=A^{\top}$. It is not $A$: the transpose comes from $G^{\top}$ in the identification formula. Likewise, $\operatorname{tr}(AX^{\top})$ has differential $\operatorname{tr}(A(dX)^{\top})=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\top}dX)$, so its gradient is $A$; the gradient of $\operatorname{tr}X$ is $I$. For $\operatorname{tr}(AX)$ one needs $A$ of size $m\times n$ and $X$ of size $n\times m$; for $\operatorname{tr}(AX^{\top})$ one needs $A,X$ both of size $m\times n$. Neither requires square matrices, only a defined trace. Conclusion: the coefficient matrix of a linear trace form is transposed when the gradient is read off; $A^{\top}$ and $A$ must not be confused.

Quadratic and bilinear forms. For $f(x)=x^{\top}Ax$, $$\begin{aligned}df&=(dx)^{\top}Ax+x^{\top}A\,dx\\&=x^{\top}A^{\top}dx+x^{\top}A\,dx\\&=x^{\top}(A+A^{\top})dx.\end{aligned}$$ so $\nabla f=(A+A^{\top})x$; it reduces to $2Ax$ only when $A=A^{\top}$. For $f(X)=a^{\top}Xb$, $$\begin{aligned}df&=a^{\top}(dX)b=\operatorname{tr}(ba^{\top}dX)\\&=\operatorname{tr}\big((ab^{\top})^{\top}dX\big).\end{aligned}$$ so $\partial(a^{\top}Xb)/\partial X=ab^{\top}$. The hypotheses are that $A$ is a real $n\times n$ matrix and $a,b$ have compatible shapes with $X$; the quadratic formula does not require symmetry of $A$, but symmetrization is mandatory. Conclusion: the outer product $ab^{\top}$ and the symmetrized $(A+A^{\top})x$ are two basic entries.

Trace-quadratic form: let $A$ be $n\times n$ and $X$ be $n\times p$, with $f=\operatorname{tr}(X^{\top}AX)$. Then $$\begin{aligned}df&=\operatorname{tr}\big((dX)^{\top}AX\big)+\operatorname{tr}\big(X^{\top}A\,dX\big)\\&=\operatorname{tr}\big(X^{\top}A^{\top}dX\big)+\operatorname{tr}\big(X^{\top}A\,dX\big)\\&=\operatorname{tr}\big(((A+A^{\top})X)^{\top}dX\big),\end{aligned}$$ so the gradient is $(A+A^{\top})X$, which becomes $2AX$ when $A$ is symmetric. The first step uses $\operatorname{tr}((dX)^{\top}AX)=\operatorname{tr}(X^{\top}A^{\top}dX)$ (a scalar equals its transpose), and the last uses the transpose of $(A+A^{\top})X$. The hypotheses are compatible shapes and differentiability. Conclusion: whether $X$ is a vector or a matrix, a quadratic form must be symmetrized in $A$ before reading the gradient.

Determinant and inverse forms ($X$ invertible). Jacobi's formula gives $d\det X=\det X\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}dX)$, and $\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}dX)=\operatorname{tr}((X^{-\top})^{\top}dX)$, hence $$\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial\det X}{\partial X}&=\det(X)\,X^{-\top},\\ \frac{\partial\ln\det X}{\partial X}&=X^{-\top}.\end{aligned}$$ For $f=\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}A)$, use $d(X^{-1})=-X^{-1}dX\,X^{-1}$: $$df=-\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}dX\,X^{-1}A)=-\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}AX^{-1}dX),$$ so $\partial f/\partial X=-X^{-\top}A^{\top}X^{-\top}$. The hypotheses are invertibility of $X$ (and $\det X>0$ for the real logarithm, e.g. positive definite $X$). Conclusion: neither transpose in the inverse formula may be dropped.

Two pitfalls. First, the formulas for $\partial\det X/\partial X$ and $\partial\ln\det X/\partial X$ above are **unconstrained** (full matrix space) versions; if $X$ is restricted to symmetric matrices, the tangent space contains only symmetric directions, and the intrinsic gradient is the symmetric part $\operatorname{sym}(G)=(G+G^{\top})/2$, because $\operatorname{tr}(G^{\top}dX)$ sees only the symmetric part of $dX$. For symmetric invertible $X$, $\det X\,X^{-\top}=\det X\,X^{-1}$ is already symmetric, so that entry is unchanged; but the intrinsic gradient of $\operatorname{tr}(AX)$ on the symmetric subspace is $(A+A^{\top})/2$, not $A^{\top}$. Second, every result can be checked by finite differences: for any $B$, compare $(f(X+tB)-f(X))/t$ with $\operatorname{tr}(G^{\top}B)$. The hypothesis is that the inner product and tangent space on the constrained manifold are fixed. Conclusion: decide first whether the problem is constrained, then apply a formula.

设 $f:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}$ 在 $x^{*}$ 处可微，且 $x^{*}$ 是定义域的内点、局部极小点。对任意方向 $d$，一元函数 $\varphi(t)=f(x^{*}+td)$ 在 $t=0$ 取局部极小，故 $$0=\varphi'(0)=
abla f(x^{*})^{	op}d.$$ 该式对所有 $d$ 成立，取 $d=
abla f(x^{*})$ 得 $\|
abla f(x^{*})\|^{2}=0$，即 $
abla f(x^{*})=0$。条件是内点与可微性；边界点的一阶条件要换成可行方向或 KKT 条件。结论：驻点是局部极值的必要条件，但非充分条件（鞍点也满足）。

设 $f$ 在 $x^{*}$ 的邻域内 $C^{2}$，Hessian $H(x)=\partial^{2}f/\partial x\,\partial x^{\top}$ 连续，故对称。若 $\nabla f(x^{*})=0$，Taylor 展开为 $$f(x^{*}+td)=f(x^{*})+\frac{t^{2}}{2}d^{\top}H(x^{*})d+o(t^{2}).$$ 若 $H(x^{*})\succ0$，则 $d^{\top}Hd\ge\lambda_{\min}\|d\|^{2}>0$，对小 $t\ne0$ 有 $f(x^{*}+td)>f(x^{*})$，故为严格局部极小；$H\prec0$ 时为严格局部极大。若 $H$ 不定，取 $d_{+},d_{-}$ 使其二次型分别为正、负，则沿两方向的函数值一增一减，$x^{*}$ 是鞍点。条件是 $C^{2}$ 与 $H$ 的定号性；$H$ 半正定（含 $H=0$）时此判据失效。结论：正定、负定、不定分别给出严格极小、严格极大、鞍点，但正定只是充分条件。

无约束二次型：取 $A=A^{	op}\in\mathbb{R}^{n	imes n}$、$b\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$，$$f(x)=x^{	op}Ax-b^{	op}x.$$ 由 $
abla(x^{	op}Ax)=(A+A^{	op})x=2Ax$、$
abla(b^{	op}x)=b$，得 $$
abla f=2Ax-b,\qquad H=2A.$$ 令梯度为零得 $Ax=b/2$；当 $A\succ0$ 时 $A$ 可逆且 $H\succ0$，唯一全局极小点为 $$x^{*}= rac12A^{-1}b,\qquad f(x^{*})=- rac14b^{	op}A^{-1}b.$$ 条件是 $A$ 对称；正定性保证唯一极小，$A$ 不定时驻点是鞍点，$A$ 半正定奇异时需另行分析。结论：二次型的梯度、Hessian 与极小点都是整块公式。

最小二乘：$A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$、$b\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$，$$f(x)=\|Ax-b\|^{2}=x^{\top}A^{\top}Ax-2b^{\top}Ax+b^{\top}b.$$ 由二次型公式（$A^{\top}A$ 对称）得 $$\nabla f=2A^{\top}Ax-2A^{\top}b=2A^{\top}(Ax-b),\qquad H=2A^{\top}A\succeq0.$$ 令梯度为零得正规方程 $$A^{\top}Ax=A^{\top}b.$$ 它总有解，因为 $A^{\top}b\in\operatorname{range}(A^{\top})=\operatorname{range}(A^{\top}A)$。若 $A$ 列满秩，$A^{\top}A\succ0$，解唯一：$$x^{*}=(A^{\top}A)^{-1}A^{\top}b;$$ 若秩亏，解集是仿射子空间，广义逆给出最小范数解 $A^{+}b$。条件：$A$ 实矩阵、$b$ 同维；列满秩才保证唯一。结论：正规方程是最小二乘的一阶条件，Hessian 半正定保证凸性。

用正交性证明最优：设 $x$ 满足正规方程，令 $r=b-Ax$，则 $A^{\top}r=0$。对任意 $z$，$$\begin{aligned}f(x+z)&=\|r-Az\|^{2}\\&=\|r\|^{2}-2r^{\top}Az+\|Az\|^{2}\\&=f(x)+\|Az\|^{2}\ge f(x),\end{aligned}$$ 其中交叉项 $r^{\top}Az=(A^{\top}r)^{\top}z=0$。故 $x$ 是全局极小点；等号成立当且仅当 $Az=0$。几何上 $r\perp\operatorname{col}(A)$，$Ax$ 是 $b$ 在列空间上的正交投影。条件：$x$ 满足正规方程；列满秩时 $Az\ne0$（$z\ne0$），极小点唯一。结论：正规方程不仅是一阶必要条件，也直接给出全局最优性。

半正定的细微差别与二阶条件的方向。若 $f$ 在 $x^{*}$ 局部极小且 $C^{2}$，则必有 $H(x^{*})\succeq0$（否则沿负曲率方向 $d^{\top}Hd<0$，$f$ 会下降），这是二阶必要条件；但 $H\succ0$ 只是严格极小的充分条件，不是必要条件。反例 $f(x)=x^{4}$ 在 $x=0$：$f'=4x^{3}$、$f''=12x^{2}$，故 $H(0)=0$ 半正定，而 $0$ 仍是严格极小点，需看更高阶项。反过来，$f(x)=x^{3}$ 在 $0$ 处同样 $H(0)=0$，但 $0$ 不是极小点，所以半正定本身也不充分。数值上一阶方法用 $x_{k+1}=x_{k}-\eta\nabla f(x_{k})$，牛顿法在 $H\succ0$ 时用方向 $-H^{-1}\nabla f$。条件是 $C^{2}$ 保证 $H$ 对称。结论：在驻点处，$H$ 正定 $\Rightarrow$ 严格极小；局部极小 $\Rightarrow$ $H$ 半正定；反向蕴含均不成立。
en:
Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $x^{*}$, an interior point of its domain and a local minimum. For every direction $d$, the one-variable function $\varphi(t)=f(x^{*}+td)$ has a local minimum at $t=0$, so $$0=\varphi'(0)=
abla f(x^{*})^{	op}d.$$ This holds for all $d$; taking $d=
abla f(x^{*})$ gives $\|
abla f(x^{*})\|^{2}=0$, hence $
abla f(x^{*})=0$. The hypotheses are an interior point and differentiability; at a boundary point the first-order condition is replaced by feasible directions or KKT conditions. Conclusion: a stationary point is necessary for a local extremum, but not sufficient (saddles also satisfy it).

Assume $f$ is $C^{2}$ near $x^{*}$, with continuous Hessian $H(x)=\partial^{2}f/\partial x\,\partial x^{\top}$, which is therefore symmetric. If $\nabla f(x^{*})=0$, Taylor's expansion gives $$f(x^{*}+td)=f(x^{*})+\frac{t^{2}}{2}d^{\top}H(x^{*})d+o(t^{2}).$$ If $H(x^{*})\succ0$, then $d^{\top}Hd\ge\lambda_{\min}\|d\|^{2}>0$, so $f(x^{*}+td)>f(x^{*})$ for small $t\ne0$: a strict local minimum. If $H\prec0$, it is a strict local maximum. If $H$ is indefinite, choose $d_{+},d_{-}$ making the quadratic form positive and negative; along these directions $f$ increases and decreases, so $x^{*}$ is a saddle. The hypotheses are $C^{2}$ and a definite sign of $H$; when $H$ is only positive semidefinite (including $H=0$), this test is inconclusive. Conclusion: positive definite, negative definite and indefinite give a strict minimum, a strict maximum and a saddle respectively, but positive definiteness is only sufficient.

Unconstrained quadratic form: take $A=A^{	op}\in\mathbb{R}^{n	imes n}$ and $b\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$, $$f(x)=x^{	op}Ax-b^{	op}x.$$ Since $
abla(x^{	op}Ax)=(A+A^{	op})x=2Ax$ and $
abla(b^{	op}x)=b$, $$
abla f=2Ax-b,\qquad H=2A.$$ Setting the gradient to zero gives $Ax=b/2$; when $A\succ0$, $A$ is invertible and $H\succ0$, so the unique global minimizer is $$x^{*}= rac12A^{-1}b,\qquad f(x^{*})=- rac14b^{	op}A^{-1}b.$$ The hypothesis is symmetry of $A$; positive definiteness guarantees a unique minimum, an indefinite $A$ makes the stationary point a saddle, and a singular positive semidefinite $A$ needs separate analysis. Conclusion: the gradient, Hessian and minimizer of a quadratic form are all block formulas.

Least squares: $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $b\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$, $$f(x)=\|Ax-b\|^{2}=x^{\top}A^{\top}Ax-2b^{\top}Ax+b^{\top}b.$$ The quadratic formula (with $A^{\top}A$ symmetric) gives $$\nabla f=2A^{\top}Ax-2A^{\top}b=2A^{\top}(Ax-b),\qquad H=2A^{\top}A\succeq0.$$ Setting the gradient to zero yields the normal equations $$A^{\top}Ax=A^{\top}b.$$ They are always consistent, because $A^{\top}b\in\operatorname{range}(A^{\top})=\operatorname{range}(A^{\top}A)$. If $A$ has full column rank, $A^{\top}A\succ0$ and the solution is unique: $$x^{*}=(A^{\top}A)^{-1}A^{\top}b;$$ if $A$ is rank deficient, the solution set is an affine subspace and the pseudoinverse selects the least-norm solution $A^{+}b$. The hypotheses are a real $A$ and a compatible $b$; uniqueness requires full column rank. Conclusion: the normal equations are the first-order condition for least squares, and the positive semidefinite Hessian guarantees convexity.

Optimality via orthogonality: let $x$ satisfy the normal equations and set $r=b-Ax$, so $A^{\top}r=0$. For any $z$, $$\begin{aligned}f(x+z)&=\|r-Az\|^{2}\\&=\|r\|^{2}-2r^{\top}Az+\|Az\|^{2}\\&=f(x)+\|Az\|^{2}\ge f(x),\end{aligned}$$ because the cross term $r^{\top}Az=(A^{\top}r)^{\top}z=0$. Hence $x$ is a global minimizer, with equality iff $Az=0$. Geometrically, $r\perp\operatorname{col}(A)$ and $Ax$ is the orthogonal projection of $b$ onto the column space. The hypothesis is that $x$ satisfies the normal equations; with full column rank, $Az\ne0$ for $z\ne0$ and the minimizer is unique. Conclusion: the normal equations are not only necessary but directly imply global optimality.

The positive-semidefinite subtlety and the direction of the second-order conditions. If $f$ has a local minimum at $x^{*}$ and is $C^{2}$, then necessarily $H(x^{*})\succeq0$ (otherwise $f$ decreases along a direction with $d^{\top}Hd<0$); this is the second-order necessary condition. But $H\succ0$ is only sufficient for a strict minimum, not necessary. Counterexample: $f(x)=x^{4}$ at $x=0$ has $f'=4x^{3}$ and $f''=12x^{2}$, so $H(0)=0$ is positive semidefinite, yet $0$ is still a strict minimum; higher-order terms decide. Conversely, $f(x)=x^{3}$ at $0$ also has $H(0)=0$, but $0$ is not a minimum, so positive semidefiniteness alone is not sufficient either. Numerically, first-order methods iterate $x_{k+1}=x_{k}-\eta\nabla f(x_{k})$, while Newton's method uses the direction $-H^{-1}\nabla f$ when $H\succ0$. The hypothesis $C^{2}$ makes $H$ symmetric. Conclusion: at a stationary point, $H$ positive definite $\Rightarrow$ strict minimum, and a local minimum $\Rightarrow$ $H$ positive semidefinite; neither converse holds.

zh: 设 $A(t)$ 可微，$\lambda(t)$ 是 $A(t)$ 的一个**单重**特征值（代数重数 1），$v(t)$ 是对应的单位特征向量：$A(t)v(t)=\lambda(t)v(t)$、$v(t)^{\top}v(t)=1$。单重性保证特征值分支与特征向量可选取为可微（Kato 扰动定理）。对恒等式求导：$$\dot A v+A\dot v=\dot\lambda v+\lambda\dot v.$$ 左乘 $v^{\top}$，得 $$v^{\top}\dot A v+v^{\top}A\dot v=\dot\lambda\,v^{\top}v+\lambda\,v^{\top}\dot v.$$ 对称情形 $A=A^{\top}$ 且扰动 $dA=dA^{\top}$ 有 $v^{\top}A=\lambda v^{\top}$，且 $v^{\top}v=1$，故 $\lambda v^{\top}\dot v$ 两项相消，$\dot\lambda=v^{\top}\dot A v$。结论：在对称矩阵空间内 $d\lambda=v^{\top}(dA)v$，其中 $dA$ 对称。

把方向导数写成迹形式：$$\begin{aligned}d\lambda&=v^{\top}(dA)v=\operatorname{tr}(v^{\top}(dA)v)\\&=\operatorname{tr}(vv^{\top}dA)=\operatorname{tr}\big((vv^{\top})^{\top}dA\big).\end{aligned}$$ 与 $df=\operatorname{tr}(G^{\top}dA)$ 对照，得 $$\frac{\partial\lambda}{\partial A}=vv^{\top}.$$ 该梯度对称、半正定、秩一、迹为 1，正是向 $v$ 的正交投影；$v\to-v$ 时 $vv^{\top}$ 不变，符合特征值不依赖特征向量符号。条件是实对称、扰动 $dA$ 对称（Hermitian 情形把转置换成共轭转置、用 $v^{*}$）且 $\lambda$ 单重。结论：对称情形特征值梯度是秩一投影。

非对称矩阵需要左右特征向量：右特征向量 $Av=\lambda v$，左特征向量 $w^{\top}A=\lambda w^{\top}$，并取 $\lambda$ 单重。对 $Av=\lambda v$ 求导并左乘 $w^{\top}$：$$w^{\top}\dot A v+w^{\top}A\dot v=\dot\lambda\,w^{\top}v+\lambda\,w^{\top}\dot v.$$ 由 $w^{\top}A=\lambda w^{\top}$，第二项相消，故 $$\dot\lambda=\frac{w^{\top}\dot A v}{w^{\top}v}.$$ 单重性保证 $w^{\top}v\ne0$；公式对 $v$、$w$ 各自的非零伸缩不变。写成微分与梯度：$$\begin{aligned}d\lambda&=\frac{w^{\top}(dA)v}{w^{\top}v},\\ \frac{\partial\lambda}{\partial A}&=\frac{wv^{\top}}{w^{\top}v}.\end{aligned}$$ 条件：$\lambda$ 单重；对称情形 $w=v$ 退化为 $vv^{\top}$。结论：一般矩阵的特征值梯度是秩一但非对称的矩阵。

奇异值：设 $\sigma>0$ 是 $A$ 的单重奇异值，$u,v$ 为单位左、右奇异向量：$$Av=\sigma u,\qquad A^{\top}u=\sigma v,\qquad \|u\|=\|v\|=1.$$ 对第一式求导并左乘 $u^{\top}$：$$u^{\top}\dot A v+u^{\top}A\dot v=\dot\sigma\,u^{\top}u+\sigma\,u^{\top}\dot u.$$ 由 $A^{\top}u=\sigma v$ 得 $u^{\top}A=\sigma v^{\top}$，故 $u^{\top}A\dot v=\sigma v^{\top}\dot v=0$；又 $u^{\top}\dot u=0$（单位向量），所以 $$\dot\sigma=u^{\top}\dot A v,\qquad d\sigma=u^{\top}(dA)v.$$ 与 $d\sigma=\operatorname{tr}((uv^{\top})^{\top}dA)$ 对照得 $\partial\sigma/\partial A=uv^{\top}$。条件是 $\sigma>0$ 且单重（保证 $u,v$ 可微且符号可固定）；$\sigma=0$ 处公式不成立。结论：正奇异值的梯度是 $uv^{\top}$，式中没有绝对值；$uv^{\top}$ 在同时变号 $(u,v)\to(-u,-v)$ 下不变。单独翻转一个奇异向量会改变 $uv^{\top}$ 的符号并破坏奇异向量方程，因此配对奇异向量只有公共符号自由。

条件失效的反例。特征值：$A(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t,-t)$ 的特征值为 $t,-t$，最大特征值 $\lambda_{\max}(t)=|t|$ 在 $t=0$ 有折点，不可微；此时 $t=0$ 处特征值 $0$ 是二重的，单重前提不成立。若 $A(t)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\t&0\end{pmatrix}$，特征多项式为 $\lambda^{2}-t=0$，特征值 $\pm\sqrt t$（$t\ge0$）在 $0$ 处出现 $t^{1/2}$ 行为，正对应 $t=0$ 处 Jordan 块大小为 2 的分数幂展开。奇异值：$A(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t,0)$ 的奇异值为 $|t|,0$，在 $t=0$ 处 $\sigma_1=\sigma_2=0$ 既为零又二重；$|t|$ 只有单侧导数 $\pm1$，而 $u^{\top}\dot A v=1$ 只对应 $t>0$ 的一侧。结论：重特征值、重奇异值或 $\sigma=0$ 处一阶公式一般不能套用，至少要逐例检查；此时最多谈方向导数或分叉。

谱函数组合：设 $A=A^{\top}$ 的特征值 $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ 单重，$V=[v_1\ \cdots\ v_n]$ 正交，$f(A)=g(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$，$g$ 对称且可微。由 $d\lambda_i=v_i^{\top}dA\,v_i$，$$\begin{aligned}df&=\sum_i\frac{\partial g}{\partial\lambda_i}v_i^{\top}dA\,v_i\\&=\operatorname{tr}\left(\left(\sum_i\frac{\partial g}{\partial\lambda_i}v_iv_i^{\top}\right)^{\top}dA\right),\end{aligned}$$ 故 $$\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial A}&=\sum_i\frac{\partial g}{\partial\lambda_i}v_iv_i^{\top}\\&=V\operatorname{diag}(\nabla_\lambda g)V^{\top}.\end{aligned}$$ 例：$g=\sum_i\lambda_i^{2}$ 给出 $2A$；$g=\sum_i\ln\lambda_i$（$A\succ0$）给出 $A^{-1}$。另 $d\|A\|_F^{2}=2\operatorname{tr}(A^{\top}dA)$，梯度 $2A$，完全不需要 SVD。条件是对称扰动下谱单重时逐特征值推导；若特征值重合但 $g$ 对称，谱函数仍可能光滑，需用 Daleckii–Krein 或矩阵函数理论，不能硬套单个 $\lambda_i$ 的导数。结论：谱函数梯度按特征投影加权；单个特征值公式在单重时保证可用，重根处一般失效，不能硬套。
en: Let $A(t)$ be differentiable and let $\lambda(t)$ be a **simple** eigenvalue (algebraic multiplicity one) with unit eigenvector $v(t)$: $A(t)v(t)=\lambda(t)v(t)$ and $v(t)^{\top}v(t)=1$. Simplicity guarantees that the eigenvalue branch and the eigenvector can be chosen differentiable (Kato perturbation theory). Differentiating the identity gives $$\dot A v+A\dot v=\dot\lambda v+\lambda\dot v.$$ Multiplying on the left by $v^{\top}$, $$v^{\top}\dot A v+v^{\top}A\dot v=\dot\lambda\,v^{\top}v+\lambda\,v^{\top}\dot v.$$ In the symmetric case $A=A^{\top}$ with a symmetric perturbation $dA=dA^{\top}$, $v^{\top}A=\lambda v^{\top}$, and $v^{\top}v=1$, so the two $\lambda v^{\top}\dot v$ terms cancel and $\dot\lambda=v^{\top}\dot A v$. Conclusion: within the symmetric-matrix space, $d\lambda=v^{\top}(dA)v$ with $dA$ symmetric.

Write the directional derivative in trace form: $$\begin{aligned}d\lambda&=v^{\top}(dA)v=\operatorname{tr}(v^{\top}(dA)v)\\&=\operatorname{tr}(vv^{\top}dA)=\operatorname{tr}\big((vv^{\top})^{\top}dA\big).\end{aligned}$$ Comparison with $df=\operatorname{tr}(G^{\top}dA)$ gives $$\frac{\partial\lambda}{\partial A}=vv^{\top}.$$ This gradient is symmetric, positive semidefinite, rank one and has trace one — the orthogonal projector onto $v$. It is unchanged by $v\to-v$, consistent with the eigenvalue being independent of the eigenvector's sign. The hypotheses are real symmetry, a symmetric perturbation $dA$, and simplicity of $\lambda$ (in the Hermitian case replace transposes by conjugate transposes and use $v^{*}$). Conclusion: for a symmetric matrix the eigenvalue gradient is a rank-one projector.

A non-symmetric matrix requires left and right eigenvectors: $Av=\lambda v$ and $w^{\top}A=\lambda w^{\top}$, with $\lambda$ simple. Differentiate $Av=\lambda v$ and multiply on the left by $w^{\top}$: $$w^{\top}\dot A v+w^{\top}A\dot v=\dot\lambda\,w^{\top}v+\lambda\,w^{\top}\dot v.$$ Since $w^{\top}A=\lambda w^{\top}$, the second terms cancel, hence $$\dot\lambda=\frac{w^{\top}\dot A v}{w^{\top}v}.$$ Simplicity guarantees $w^{\top}v\ne0$, and the formula is invariant under separate nonzero rescalings of $v$ and $w$. In differential and gradient form, $$\begin{aligned}d\lambda&=\frac{w^{\top}(dA)v}{w^{\top}v},\\ \frac{\partial\lambda}{\partial A}&=\frac{wv^{\top}}{w^{\top}v}.\end{aligned}$$ The hypothesis is simplicity of $\lambda$; in the symmetric case $w=v$ and this reduces to $vv^{\top}$. Conclusion: for a general matrix the eigenvalue gradient is rank one but non-symmetric.

Singular values: let $\sigma>0$ be a simple singular value of $A$, with unit left and right singular vectors $u,v$: $$Av=\sigma u,\qquad A^{\top}u=\sigma v,\qquad \|u\|=\|v\|=1.$$ Differentiate the first equation and multiply on the left by $u^{\top}$: $$u^{\top}\dot A v+u^{\top}A\dot v=\dot\sigma\,u^{\top}u+\sigma\,u^{\top}\dot u.$$ From $A^{\top}u=\sigma v$ we get $u^{\top}A=\sigma v^{\top}$, so $u^{\top}A\dot v=\sigma v^{\top}\dot v=0$; also $u^{\top}\dot u=0$ because $u$ is a unit vector. Hence $$\dot\sigma=u^{\top}\dot A v,\qquad d\sigma=u^{\top}(dA)v.$$ Comparison with $d\sigma=\operatorname{tr}((uv^{\top})^{\top}dA)$ gives $\partial\sigma/\partial A=uv^{\top}$. The hypotheses are $\sigma>0$ and simplicity (which makes $u,v$ differentiable with fixed signs); the formula fails at $\sigma=0$. Conclusion: the gradient of a positive singular value is $uv^{\top}$, with no absolute value in the formula; $uv^{\top}$ is unchanged under the simultaneous sign flip $(u,v)\to(-u,-v)$. Flipping only one singular vector changes the sign of $uv^{\top}$ and breaks the singular-vector equations, so a paired singular-vector pair has only common sign freedom.

Counterexamples when the hypotheses fail. Eigenvalues: $A(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t,-t)$ has eigenvalues $t,-t$, and its largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\max}(t)=|t|$ has a kink at $t=0$, so it is not differentiable; at $t=0$ the eigenvalue $0$ is repeated, violating simplicity. For $A(t)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\t&0\end{pmatrix}$ the characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^{2}-t=0$, so the eigenvalues are $\pm\sqrt t$ for $t\ge0$ and exhibit $t^{1/2}$ behavior at $0$, matching the fractional-power expansion for a Jordan block of size 2 at $t=0$. Singular values: $A(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t,0)$ has singular values $|t|,0$; at $t=0$, $\sigma_1=\sigma_2=0$ is both zero and repeated, $|t|$ has only the one-sided derivatives $\pm1$, and $u^{\top}\dot A v=1$ corresponds only to the side $t>0$. Conclusion: at repeated eigenvalues, repeated singular values or $\sigma=0$, first-order formulas generally cannot be applied without a case-by-case check; at most one speaks of directional derivatives or branching.

Spectral composition: let $A=A^{\top}$ have simple eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$, let $V=[v_1\ \cdots\ v_n]$ be orthogonal, and let $f(A)=g(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$ with $g$ symmetric and differentiable. From $d\lambda_i=v_i^{\top}dA\,v_i$, $$\begin{aligned}df&=\sum_i\frac{\partial g}{\partial\lambda_i}v_i^{\top}dA\,v_i\\&=\operatorname{tr}\left(\left(\sum_i\frac{\partial g}{\partial\lambda_i}v_iv_i^{\top}\right)^{\top}dA\right),\end{aligned}$$ hence $$\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial A}&=\sum_i\frac{\partial g}{\partial\lambda_i}v_iv_i^{\top}\\&=V\operatorname{diag}(\nabla_\lambda g)V^{\top}.\end{aligned}$$ For example, $g=\sum_i\lambda_i^{2}$ gives $2A$, and $g=\sum_i\ln\lambda_i$ for $A\succ0$ gives $A^{-1}$. Separately, $d\|A\|_F^{2}=2\operatorname{tr}(A^{\top}dA)$ has gradient $2A$ and requires no SVD. The hypothesis is a simple spectrum under symmetric perturbations for the eigenvalue-by-eigenvalue derivation; if eigenvalues coincide but $g$ is symmetric, the spectral function may still be smooth and one needs Daleckii–Krein or matrix-function theory rather than the derivative of an individual $\lambda_i$. Conclusion: spectral gradients weight eigenprojectors; the single-eigenvalue formula is guaranteed under simplicity and generally fails at repeated eigenvalues, so it must not be applied blindly.

zh: 先看幂：对可微的 $X(t)$，由乘积法则归纳得 $$d(X^{k})=\sum_{a=0}^{k-1}X^{a}(dX)X^{k-1-a}\qquad(k\ge1).$$ 例如 $d(X^{2})=(dX)X+X(dX)$，一般不等于 $2X\,dX$。当 $X\,dX=dX\,X$ 时，各项相同，公式化为 $d(X^{k})=kX^{k-1}dX$；不交换时不能这样化简。条件是 $X(t)$ 可微、幂有定义；不需要 $X$ 可逆。结论：非交换性是矩阵函数求导与标量求导的根本差异，任何简化前先检查 $X$ 与 $dX$ 是否交换。

矩阵指数由幂级数定义：$e^{X}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}X^{k}/k!$，在紧集上一致收敛，可逐项微分。于是 $$d e^{X}=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k!}\sum_{a+b=k-1}X^{a}(dX)X^{b}.$$ 将其与积分 $$L_{\exp}(X,dX)=\int_0^1 e^{sX}(dX)e^{(1-s)X}\,ds$$ 比较：展开两个指数后，$X^{a}(dX)X^{b}$ 的系数是 $$\frac{1}{a!b!}\int_0^1s^{a}(1-s)^{b}ds=\frac{1}{(a+b+1)!},$$ 正好等于幂级数求导中的系数。故对任意可微 $X(t)$，$$d e^{X}=\int_0^1e^{sX}(dX)e^{(1-s)X}\,ds,$$ 无需交换性。结论：这是 $e^{X}$ 的 Fréchet 导数 $L_{\exp}(X,\cdot)$，对扰动线性。

可交换特例：若 $X\,dX=dX\,X$，则 $e^{sX}$、$e^{(1-s)X}$ 都与 $dX$ 交换，且乘积为 $e^{X}$，被积函数与 $s$ 无关，积分化为 $$d e^{X}=e^{X}dX=dX\,e^{X}.$$ 特别地取 $X=tA$、$dX=A\,dt$，因 $A$ 与 $e^{tA}$ 恒交换，得 $$\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}=A\,e^{tA}=e^{tA}A,\qquad \frac{d^{k}}{dt^{k}}e^{tA}=A^{k}e^{tA}.$$ 这也说明 $e^{tA}$ 是线性 ODE $Y'=AY$、$Y(0)=I$ 的解，$A$ 是生成元。条件：$X$ 与 $dX$ 交换；$X=tA$ 自动满足。结论：常见的 $de^{X}=e^{X}dX$ 是可交换特例下的化简，不能当作通式。

逆矩阵：设 $X(t)$ 在讨论点可逆。对 $XX^{-1}=I$ 求导，$$\dot X X^{-1}+X\frac{d}{dt}X^{-1}=0,$$ 故 $$\frac{d}{dt}X^{-1}=-X^{-1}\dot X X^{-1},\qquad d(X^{-1})=-X^{-1}(dX)X^{-1}.$$ 可逆性在一点成立时由连续性在邻域保持，所以路径导数有意义；公式对每个可逆点逐点成立。它与标量 $(1/x)'=-x'/x^{2}$ 相容，但矩阵情形必须保留两侧的 $X^{-1}$，不能写成 $-X^{-2}dX$。结论：求逆的 Fréchet 导数由这个三因子夹心公式给出，顺序不可换。

对数与平方根。对谱在 $\mathbb{C}\setminus(-\infty,0]$ 内的 $X$，$\log X$ 的 Fréchet 导数为 $$d\log X=\int_0^1(sX+(1-s)I)^{-1}(dX)(sX+(1-s)I)^{-1}\,ds.$$ 对平方根，$d\sqrt X$ 是 Sylvester 方程 $$(d\sqrt X)\sqrt X+\sqrt X(d\sqrt X)=dX$$ 的唯一解；当 $\sqrt X$ 与 $-\sqrt X$ 的谱不相交（实对称正定时自动成立）时解唯一。若 $X$ 与 $dX$ 交换，这两式分别简化为 $$d\log X=X^{-1}dX,\qquad d\sqrt X=\frac12(\sqrt X)^{-1}dX.$$ 条件是谱落在函数定义域内、导数存在；实对称正定时 $\log$ 与 $\sqrt{}$ 都可微。结论：一般情形必须用积分或 Sylvester 方程；在可交换情形下可化简为普通的左乘 $X^{-1}$ 或 $\frac12(\sqrt X)^{-1}$。

迹与行列式的例外。对任意可微的 $X(t)$，由积分公式和迹的循环性，$$\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{tr}e^{X}&=\operatorname{tr}\left(\int_0^1e^{sX}\dot Xe^{(1-s)X}ds\right)\\&=\operatorname{tr}(e^{X}\dot X),\end{aligned}$$ 即 $d\operatorname{tr}e^{X}=\operatorname{tr}(e^{X}dX)$；按分母布局，梯度为 $(e^{X})^{\top}$。对可逆 $X$，Jacobi 公式给出 $$d\det X=\det(X)\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}dX),$$ 与矩阵函数是否可交换无关，只要求 $X$ 可逆。条件是 $X$ 可微；行列式公式额外要求可逆。结论：非交换性使 $de^{X}$ 变复杂，但迹与行列式仍保持简洁，可作为检验一般公式的基准。
en: Start with powers: for differentiable $X(t)$, induction on the product rule gives $$d(X^{k})=\sum_{a=0}^{k-1}X^{a}(dX)X^{k-1-a}\qquad(k\ge1).$$ For example, $d(X^{2})=(dX)X+X(dX)$, which is not $2X\,dX$ in general. When $X\,dX=dX\,X$, all terms coincide and the formula collapses to $d(X^{k})=kX^{k-1}dX$; without commutativity this simplification is invalid. The hypotheses are differentiability of $X(t)$ and defined powers; invertibility of $X$ is not required. Conclusion: noncommutativity is the fundamental difference from scalar calculus, and every simplification must be preceded by a check whether $X$ and $dX$ commute.

The matrix exponential is defined by the power series $e^{X}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}X^{k}/k!$, which converges uniformly on compact sets and may be differentiated termwise. Hence $$d e^{X}=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k!}\sum_{a+b=k-1}X^{a}(dX)X^{b}.$$ Compare this with the integral $$L_{\exp}(X,dX)=\int_0^1 e^{sX}(dX)e^{(1-s)X}\,ds.$$ Expanding the two exponentials, the coefficient of $X^{a}(dX)X^{b}$ is $$\frac{1}{a!b!}\int_0^1s^{a}(1-s)^{b}ds=\frac{1}{(a+b+1)!},$$ exactly the coefficient in the differentiated series. Therefore, for every differentiable $X(t)$, $$d e^{X}=\int_0^1e^{sX}(dX)e^{(1-s)X}\,ds,$$ with no commutativity assumption. Conclusion: this is the Fréchet derivative $L_{\exp}(X,\cdot)$ of $e^{X}$, linear in the perturbation.

Commuting special case: if $X\,dX=dX\,X$, then $e^{sX}$ and $e^{(1-s)X}$ commute with $dX$, their product is $e^{X}$, and the integrand is independent of $s$; the integral becomes $$d e^{X}=e^{X}dX=dX\,e^{X}.$$ In particular, take $X=tA$ and $dX=A\,dt$; since $A$ always commutes with $e^{tA}$, $$\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}=A\,e^{tA}=e^{tA}A,\qquad \frac{d^{k}}{dt^{k}}e^{tA}=A^{k}e^{tA}.$$ This also shows that $e^{tA}$ solves the linear ODE $Y'=AY$, $Y(0)=I$, with generator $A$. The hypothesis is that $X$ and $dX$ commute; $X=tA$ satisfies it automatically. Conclusion: the familiar $de^{X}=e^{X}dX$ is a simplification available in the commuting special case, not a general formula.

Inverse: let $X(t)$ be invertible at the point under discussion. Differentiating $XX^{-1}=I$ gives $$\dot X X^{-1}+X\frac{d}{dt}X^{-1}=0,$$ hence $$\frac{d}{dt}X^{-1}=-X^{-1}\dot X X^{-1},\qquad d(X^{-1})=-X^{-1}(dX)X^{-1}.$$ Invertibility at one point persists in a neighborhood by continuity, so the path derivative is meaningful; the formula holds pointwise at every invertible point. It is consistent with the scalar rule $(1/x)'=-x'/x^{2}$, but in the matrix case both factors $X^{-1}$ must be kept and the result cannot be written as $-X^{-2}dX$. Conclusion: the Fréchet derivative of the inverse is given by this three-factor sandwich, and the order cannot be changed.

Logarithm and square root. For $X$ with spectrum in $\mathbb{C}\setminus(-\infty,0]$, the Fréchet derivative of $\log X$ is $$d\log X=\int_0^1(sX+(1-s)I)^{-1}(dX)(sX+(1-s)I)^{-1}\,ds.$$ For the square root, $d\sqrt X$ is the unique solution of the Sylvester equation $$(d\sqrt X)\sqrt X+\sqrt X(d\sqrt X)=dX,$$ with uniqueness guaranteed when the spectra of $\sqrt X$ and $-\sqrt X$ are disjoint (automatic for real symmetric positive definite $X$). If $X$ and $dX$ commute, these formulas simplify to $$d\log X=X^{-1}dX,\qquad d\sqrt X=\frac12(\sqrt X)^{-1}dX.$$ The hypotheses are that the spectrum lies in the domain of the function and the derivative exists; for real symmetric positive definite $X$, both $\log$ and $\sqrt{}$ are differentiable. Conclusion: the general case requires the integral or the Sylvester equation; in the commuting case the formulas reduce to left multiplication by $X^{-1}$ or $\frac12(\sqrt X)^{-1}$.

The trace and determinant are exceptional. For every differentiable $X(t)$, the integral formula and cyclicity of the trace give $$\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{tr}e^{X}&=\operatorname{tr}\left(\int_0^1e^{sX}\dot Xe^{(1-s)X}ds\right)\\&=\operatorname{tr}(e^{X}\dot X),\end{aligned}$$ that is, $d\operatorname{tr}e^{X}=\operatorname{tr}(e^{X}dX)$; in the denominator layout the gradient is $(e^{X})^{\top}$. For invertible $X$, Jacobi's formula gives $$d\det X=\det(X)\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}dX),$$ independently of commutativity, requiring only invertibility. The hypothesis is differentiability of $X$; the determinant formula additionally requires invertibility. Conclusion: noncommutativity complicates $de^{X}$, but the trace and determinant remain simple and serve as benchmarks for general formulas.

zh: 设 $L$ 是标量目标，$Z$ 是中间矩阵，$\bar Z=\partial L/\partial Z$ 按分母布局与 $Z$ 同型，则恒有 $$dL=\operatorname{tr}(\bar Z^{\top}dZ).$$ 若 $Z=Z(X)$ 可微，把 $dZ$ 用 $dX$ 线性表示后回代，再用迹的循环性把 $dX$ 归并到一处，写成 $dL=\operatorname{tr}(\bar X^{\top}dX)$，则括号中的 $\bar X$ 就是 $\partial L/\partial X$。这套「微分—回代—识别」正是反向传播的数学形式：每层只做向量-雅可比积（VJP），不显式构造雅可比。条件是 $L$ 与各层映射可微、形状相容。结论：所有反向规则都从这一台发动机推出。

乘法 $Z=XY$：由 $dZ=(dX)Y+X\,dY$，$$\begin{aligned}dL&=\operatorname{tr}(\bar Z^{\top}(dX)Y)+\operatorname{tr}(\bar Z^{\top}X\,dY)\\&=\operatorname{tr}(Y\bar Z^{\top}dX)+\operatorname{tr}(\bar Z^{\top}X\,dY)\\&=\operatorname{tr}\big((\bar ZY^{\top})^{\top}dX\big)+\operatorname{tr}\big((X^{\top}\bar Z)^{\top}dY\big).\end{aligned}$$ 故 $$\bar X=\bar Z\,Y^{\top},\qquad \bar Y=X^{\top}\bar Z.$$ 顺序必须保持：$\bar X$ 中 $Y^{\top}$ 在右，$\bar Y$ 中 $X^{\top}$ 在左；写成 $Y^{\top}\bar Z$ 或 $\bar ZX^{\top}$ 都是错的。条件是 $X,Y$ 形状相容、映射可微。结论：乘法反向交换因子并转置，但转置只加在对方因子上。

转置与求逆。若 $Z=X^{\top}$，则 $$dL=\operatorname{tr}(\bar Z^{\top}(dX)^{\top})=\operatorname{tr}(\bar Z\,dX),$$ 故 $\bar X=\bar Z^{\top}$。若 $Z=X^{-1}$（$X$ 可逆），由 $dZ=-X^{-1}dX\,X^{-1}=-Z\,dX\,Z$，$$dL=-\operatorname{tr}(\bar Z^{\top}Z\,dX\,Z)=-\operatorname{tr}(Z\bar Z^{\top}Z\,dX),$$ 故 $$\bar X=-Z^{\top}\bar Z\,Z^{\top}=-X^{-\top}\bar Z\,X^{-\top}.$$ 两种写法等价，$X$ 记号便于核对形状，$Z$ 记号便于实现。条件是 $X$ 可逆。结论：转置的反向只再转置一次；求逆的反向是 $-X^{-\top}\bar ZX^{-\top}$，两个转置都不能漏。

三个常用标量目标。若 $z=\det X$（$X$ 可逆）、$L=L(z)$，则 $\bar z=\partial L/\partial z$，$$\begin{aligned}dL&=\bar z\det X\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}dX)\\&=\operatorname{tr}\big((\bar z\det X\,X^{-\top})^{\top}dX\big).\end{aligned}$$ 故 $\bar X=\bar z\det(X)X^{-\top}$；当 $L=z$ 时 $\bar X=\det(X)X^{-\top}$。若 $z=\operatorname{tr}(AX)$，则 $dz=\operatorname{tr}(A\,dX)$，故 $\bar X=\bar z A^{\top}$；当 $L=z$ 时 $\bar X=A^{\top}$。若 $z=x^{\top}Ax$，则 $dz=x^{\top}(A+A^{\top})dx$，故 $\bar x=\bar z(A+A^{\top})x$；$A$ 不对称时不能写成 $2Ax$。条件是 $\det$ 需要 $X$ 可逆，其余只要求形状相容。结论：行列式、迹、二次型三条规则分别携带 $X^{-\top}$、$A^{\top}$ 与对称化因子。

逐元素函数与广播。若 $z=\sigma(x)$ 逐元素作用，$z_i=\sigma(x_i)$，则 $dz_i=\sigma'(x_i)dx_i$，$$dL=\sum_i\bar z_i\sigma'(x_i)dx_i=(\bar z\odot\sigma'(x))^{\top}dx,$$ 故 $\bar x=\bar z\odot\sigma'(x)$；矩阵情形把内积换成迹，即 $dL=\operatorname{tr}\big((\bar Z\odot\sigma'(X))^{\top}dX\big)$。广播节点反向则按前向复制的方向求和：若 $Z=X+\mathbf{1}b^{\top}$，其中 $b\in\mathbb{R}^n$ 为列向量、$\mathbf{1}$ 为全 $1$ 列向量，前向把同一行复制到每一行，则 $\bar X=\bar Z$、$\bar b_j=\sum_i\bar Z_{ij}$。条件是 $\sigma$ 可微、广播形状相容。结论：逐元素链式法则是 Hadamard 乘积；广播的反向是归约求和。

与向量化雅可比的关系：令 $z=\operatorname{vec}(Z)$、$x=\operatorname{vec}(X)$，若 $J=\partial z/\partial x$ 取分子布局（$J_{ij}=\partial z_i/\partial x_j$），则 $dz=J\,dx$。于是 $$dL=\bar z^{\top}dz=\bar z^{\top}J\,dx=(J^{\top}\bar z)^{\top}dx,$$ 即 $\operatorname{vec}(\bar X)=J^{\top}\operatorname{vec}(\bar Z)$——这正是 VJP。反向模式从输出端逐层左乘 $J^{\top}$，等价于标量链式法则的分层应用；有限差分检验为 $(L(X+tE_{ij})-L(X))/t\to(\bar X)_{ij}$。条件是 $L$ 可微、$J$ 存在；布局必须与分母约定一致。结论：矩阵反向传播就是转置雅可比与梯度向量的乘积，乘法顺序与转置是唯一需要小心的地方。
en: Let $L$ be a scalar objective, $Z$ an intermediate matrix, and $\bar Z=\partial L/\partial Z$ its gradient in the denominator layout, with the same shape as $Z$. Then always $$dL=\operatorname{tr}(\bar Z^{\top}dZ).$$ If $Z=Z(X)$ is differentiable, express $dZ$ linearly in $dX$, substitute it back, and use cyclicity of the trace to collect $dX$ in one place, writing $dL=\operatorname{tr}(\bar X^{\top}dX)$; the bracket $\bar X$ is then $\partial L/\partial X$. This differentiate-substitute-identify pipeline is exactly the mathematical form of backpropagation: each layer only computes a vector-Jacobian product (VJP) and never forms a Jacobian explicitly. The hypotheses are differentiability of $L$ and of every layer map, with compatible shapes. Conclusion: every reverse rule is derived from this single engine.

Product $Z=XY$: from $dZ=(dX)Y+X\,dY$, $$\begin{aligned}dL&=\operatorname{tr}(\bar Z^{\top}(dX)Y)+\operatorname{tr}(\bar Z^{\top}X\,dY)\\&=\operatorname{tr}(Y\bar Z^{\top}dX)+\operatorname{tr}(\bar Z^{\top}X\,dY)\\&=\operatorname{tr}\big((\bar ZY^{\top})^{\top}dX\big)+\operatorname{tr}\big((X^{\top}\bar Z)^{\top}dY\big).\end{aligned}$$ Hence $$\bar X=\bar Z\,Y^{\top},\qquad \bar Y=X^{\top}\bar Z.$$ The order must be preserved: $Y^{\top}$ sits on the right in $\bar X$, and $X^{\top}$ sits on the left in $\bar Y$; writing $Y^{\top}\bar Z$ or $\bar ZX^{\top}$ is wrong. The hypotheses are compatible shapes of $X,Y$ and differentiability. Conclusion: the reverse of a product exchanges the factors and transposes them, but the transpose is attached only to the other factor.

Transpose and inverse. If $Z=X^{\top}$, then $$dL=\operatorname{tr}(\bar Z^{\top}(dX)^{\top})=\operatorname{tr}(\bar Z\,dX),$$ so $\bar X=\bar Z^{\top}$. If $Z=X^{-1}$ with $X$ invertible, then $dZ=-X^{-1}dX\,X^{-1}=-Z\,dX\,Z$, and $$dL=-\operatorname{tr}(\bar Z^{\top}Z\,dX\,Z)=-\operatorname{tr}(Z\bar Z^{\top}Z\,dX),$$ hence $$\bar X=-Z^{\top}\bar Z\,Z^{\top}=-X^{-\top}\bar Z\,X^{-\top}.$$ The two forms are equivalent: $X$-notation is convenient for shape checks and $Z$-notation for implementation. The hypothesis is invertibility of $X$. Conclusion: transposition reverses once more, and the inverse rule is $-X^{-\top}\bar ZX^{-\top}$; neither transpose may be dropped.

Three common scalar objectives. If $z=\det X$ with $X$ invertible and $L=L(z)$, then $\bar z=\partial L/\partial z$ and $$\begin{aligned}dL&=\bar z\det X\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}dX)\\&=\operatorname{tr}\big((\bar z\det X\,X^{-\top})^{\top}dX\big).\end{aligned}$$ so $\bar X=\bar z\det(X)X^{-\top}$; for $L=z$, $\bar X=\det(X)X^{-\top}$. If $z=\operatorname{tr}(AX)$, then $dz=\operatorname{tr}(A\,dX)$, so $\bar X=\bar z A^{\top}$; for $L=z$, $\bar X=A^{\top}$. If $z=x^{\top}Ax$, then $dz=x^{\top}(A+A^{\top})dx$, so $\bar x=\bar z(A+A^{\top})x$; when $A$ is not symmetric this must not be replaced by $2Ax$. The determinant rule requires invertibility of $X$; the others only require compatible shapes. Conclusion: the determinant, trace and quadratic rules carry $X^{-\top}$, $A^{\top}$ and a symmetrization factor respectively.

Elementwise functions and broadcasting. If $z=\sigma(x)$ acts elementwise, $z_i=\sigma(x_i)$, then $dz_i=\sigma'(x_i)dx_i$ and $$dL=\sum_i\bar z_i\sigma'(x_i)dx_i=(\bar z\odot\sigma'(x))^{\top}dx,$$ so $\bar x=\bar z\odot\sigma'(x)$; in the matrix case the inner product is replaced by a trace, $dL=\operatorname{tr}\big((\bar Z\odot\sigma'(X))^{\top}dX\big)$. A broadcasting node reverses by summing over the dimensions that were copied in the forward pass: if $Z=X+\mathbf{1}b^{\top}$ with $b\in\mathbb{R}^n$ a column vector and $\mathbf{1}$ the all-ones column, so that the forward pass replicates the same row across rows, then $\bar X=\bar Z$ and $\bar b_j=\sum_i\bar Z_{ij}$. The hypotheses are differentiability of $\sigma$ and compatible broadcast shapes. Conclusion: the elementwise chain rule is a Hadamard product, and the reverse of broadcasting is a reduction by summation.

Relation to the vectorized Jacobian: let $z=\operatorname{vec}(Z)$ and $x=\operatorname{vec}(X)$. If $J=\partial z/\partial x$ is the numerator-layout Jacobian with $J_{ij}=\partial z_i/\partial x_j$, then $dz=J\,dx$. Therefore $$dL=\bar z^{\top}dz=\bar z^{\top}J\,dx=(J^{\top}\bar z)^{\top}dx,$$ that is, $\operatorname{vec}(\bar X)=J^{\top}\operatorname{vec}(\bar Z)$ — precisely a VJP. Reverse mode multiplies by $J^{\top}$ layer by layer from the output backwards, which is the layered form of the scalar chain rule; the finite-difference check is $(L(X+tE_{ij})-L(X))/t\to(\bar X)_{ij}$. The hypotheses are differentiability of $L$ and existence of $J$, with a layout consistent with the denominator convention. Conclusion: matrix backpropagation is the product of a transposed Jacobian with a gradient vector, and order and transposition are the only delicate points.
